results.question:
Sarah Street XL Group plc - Chief Investment Officer: As Mike said, the past 18 months we've made a lot of progress eliminating what we view was negative financial guarantee and financial guarantee like exposures that came out of our old financial lines business. As a result of that focus, including the recent termination of the EIB contract, that now is down to just under $900 million, at $874 million. Now, within that amount, the largest transaction is actually just under $400 million which is a financial guarantee related to a Chilean toll risk. The good news here is that the issuer has already decided to be paid the debt and an omnibus agreement releasing XL from its financial guarantees has been signed and is now being held in escrow subject to the satisfaction of certain closing conditions. We expect those closing conditions to be satisfied, and if they are, within the next couple weeks, that exposure too will go away. And at that point it leaves us round about $500 million, and we will be continuing to work our way diligently through getting rid of the rest of these exposures in an economically sensible way.
Vinay Misquith Credit Suisse - Analyst: Where is the $500 million exposed?
Sarah Street XL Group plc - Chief Investment Officer: It's across a whole number of different deals. There's one large transaction which is a credit derivative which was a deal that was done a long long time ago. It's about $190 million. The underlying class role is predominantly securitized pools of (inaudible) and bonds. The transaction is passing all of its tests with the exception of one, and that test means that the cash flow is actually being redirected to XL faster than you would expect. And we stressed the deal and up to including the 2008 stress event, and we've very comfortable with the collateral. And the rest of that is actually there was a deal where no one is greater than $71 million and the average is $42 million and they are all performing appropriately.
Vinay Misquith Credit Suisse - Analyst: That's great, thank you.
Josh Shanker Deutsche Bank - Analyst: Good afternoon. My question relates to the business that you lost and that came back to you. Could you describe the competitors that took that business, and the negotiations to bring it back? And why do you think they didn't try harder to retain that business they got from you?
results.answer:
Mike McGavick XL Group plc - CEO: Let me give you a general comment on it and then ask Jamie to jump in. First, in some cases it was just a pure panic reaction to XL's situation as 2008 closed down. We would even get messages that risk managers had been overruled in their desire to stay with XL by others within the company but they really wanted to stay. Lot of mixed messages at that time. Another, at least rarely, was it somehow a rejection of XL but rather a reaction to current panicky conditions. As those conditions subsided, we often saw business come back very quickly because of that underlying depth of relationship. It wasn't so much that someone else took it from us but rather they just felt they couldn't stay with us until things improved, and when they improved they directed brokers or reached out to us and just got right back into the relationship. So it's really to us a testimony to the strength of our core book and the relationships we've built over many years through the kind of quality service and particularly claim service we provide. I would tell you it's more about that dynamic than it is about the current crazy pricing dynamic or anything else. But I will ask my colleagues to give you any further depth they'd like to give.
Dave Duclos XL Group plc - CEO Insurance Operations: Mike, just really quick from the insurance standpoint, the primary reason, Josh, for business coming back is related to service. Service, one, in terms of whoever took the business last year not performing at the level XL provided, and then also addressing the primary concern that Mike just talked about which is the capital concern which went away. I would say that the majority of business that we lost within insurance was in the first half of 2009. And just to give you some perspective, the amount that we've recaptured, if you want to use that word, is about 30%, 25% to 30%. So it's not 100%. I can tell you it's not because of pricing. It is driven because of the fact that the capital concerns are gone and our service performance.
Jamie Veghte XL Group plc - CEO Reinsurance Operations: Yes Jamie, the big positive variants in growth rate premium in our quarter was driven out of Bermuda, $26 million. About half of that was a couple new deals we found which were very attractive, and the other half were increased lines in businesses that we liked and customers that may have had some hesitation about security coming back. This has been repetitive quarter after quarter since our real recovery began about four quarters ago. And I would reiterate what Mike and Dave said. It's about our service, our reputation and the relationships we've had over the years.

On the off-balance-sheet asset with Cariparma, to be frank, what we decided to modify a little bit in the presentation of this customer savings within Cariparma is that -- to be frank, we got conscious that we had adopt not only traditional off-balance-sheet asset like mutual funds but also some assets which were kept under custody by Cariparma for some specific customers, which are yielding a very, very tiny level of margin, almost no revenues, which may be volatile. So we decided to strip these assets out of the real off-balance-sheet assets of Cariparma, and what is now presented is the level of real, I would say, off-balance-sheet assets, which are mutual funds kept for the individual and SME customers. So it's, I would say, purely technical and without any impact on the level of revenue. On the Corporate Centre, as you may see on Page 26, we have a trend. And you can see on the bar chart on the right-hand side of the page, we have a trend. But we have some volatility. So of course, we think we are on a good trend and we are comfortable with the idea of meeting the EUR 700 million threshold target for 2019. Lastly, on the RWA in the CIB division, I think we are there at the meeting point of 3 different trends. The first one and the most important is that strategically, we have decided to put in place a pick-and-choose approach towards our customers in order to keep only the customers with a profitability meeting a certain threshold. And we have also a distribute-to-originate strategy. This is working. And actually, we've been increasing the primary distribution in the second quarter as compared to the second quarter 2016 by, I think, 5 points, if I remember correctly. We have now, on the last 12 months, a primary distribution rate which stood at 37%. So this is an approach that we want to continue to develop. So these elements are, I would say, structural and will continue in the long run. Then you have 2 additional elements, which may change or may have a certain degree of volatility. I can vividly remember about a year ago we were in the same meeting -- the earning release con call I was telling all the investors that our North American operations had [touched the bottom]. results.answer: Gary Stern Asta Funding Inc. - President CEO: No, let me go into that in detail. I'm glad you asked that. When we buy portfolios, we scrub the portfolios immediately to see if there are any 7's or 13's. We have put back rights, and what we have done in the past and will continue to do, is put back the 7's and 13's and we get paid immediately on those. Depending on the price we pay, some of the 13's we keep if we feel they're going to, over a three-to-five-year period, collect out more than we pay for it -- which is most of the time, by the way. Historically, if you want to look at the statistics, I would say one can recover. And this is just a general average, if you look at all the 13's. One would recover approximately 20% to 25% over a five-year period -- on unsecured chapter 13's. So many times we keep the 13's and put the 7's back for repurchase. Then, as -- why I believe strongly that this will be a positive for Asta, is because as we -- first of all, our book-of-business -- there will be less chapter 7's filed than 13's for the present book-of-business we have. And the bankruptcies are not a material part of our portfolios, so I don't want anyone on on the phone to get the wrong impression. So we feel we will benefit by less people filing bankruptcy, because they don't want to pay for consumer credit counseling, and if they do file bankruptcy, there will be more 13's than 7's. And according to the American Bankruptcy Institute, presently 70% of the individuals that file bankruptcy file 7, versus 30% for 13. We definitely feel that ratio will switch and shift the other way. Angela Levy JP Morgan - Analyst: Hi. It's Angie again. Just a quick question in regards to franchise. Can you remind us again how you define a plastic franchise and what exactly that entails?
Tony Allott Silgan Holdings - President: Yes. Basically, the way we define that is around the -- those markets that are looking for a custom, highly decorated-type container. So, it's not just personal care. What's happened, of course, that's drifted us over many years into personal care because that's an area where the price point is high enough in the end consumer product that differentiating on the shelf is an important attribute. But that's not the only place. <NEWLINE> Certainly, there are examples of household chemicals and food, pet food, et cetera, where that also has been an important attribute. Angela Levy JP Morgan - Analyst: And by market, you define it as individual -- or like product line versus geographic?
Tony Allott Silgan Holdings - President: Yes, yes, yes.
Angela Levy JP Morgan - Analyst: Okay. Thank you.
Tony Allott Silgan Holdings - President: Thank you, Angela.
Tony Allott Silgan Holdings - President: I'm not sure we can break, numerically, any more for you, but are we done on the pass through, the answer to that's no. And that continues on. We have higher costs in all of our businesses that are being passed through compared to prior years. So, you'll continue to see a top-line impact from that.
Tony Allott Silgan Holdings - President: Great question. Where we stand today is we're not solidly over 50% of the cans we sell are sold with a convenience end on it or what we call quick top ends. And for us, the family of quick top ends covers aluminum, easy open ends to steel to our Dot Top and pop-and-pour-type. So, it covers -- it's a pretty broad family that is a quick top end. And so, now it's more than 50% of what we do. What we have seen clearly is that consumers do value convenience. And we've seen -- initially, we had done consumer studies that had found, gotten a pretty strong read on that. Interestingly, we used that to help design some of our products as well. <NEWLINE> But much more recently, what we've seen is that markets that have moved into a quick top end have -- the first player that goes in has seen fairly significant market share gains. And then, even the second player who goes in also has seen market share gains. And ultimately, what we've seen is the market that has moved thus far is a change in the trend of that market, an increase in demand, if you will, to that marketplace. So, as a result of that, we continue to believe other markets will look at this and certainly that seems to be the body language out there. Timing is the tricky part. It's very hard to figure out when that will happen, but we're confident enough about this that we've actually decided to move forward on other unit of capacity in support of further transitions.
Tony Allott Silgan Holdings - President: Well, moving one more unit of capacity is something like 5% of an annual CapEx.
Tony Allott Silgan Holdings - President: Yes, we're not going to go there, but the point of it is, basically, that the return you get on the asset ...
Tony Allott Silgan Holdings - President: ... Is very consistent with the return we get. So, you've got to spend a lot more capital and you get a return. Obviously, I mean, there is some margin, if you will, but it's just, in many ways it's paying the capital. And so, on a return base, it's consistent with the rest of our business.

If I take a look at the 15 or so cracker announcements that have happened in the US, it seems that only three have started construction, right? But yet there seems to be this perception that there's going to be this flood of capacity coming on stream in 2017. Could you broadly give us your view of supply/demand and more specifically of what we should expect, ex-Dow in terms of cracker delays?
results.answer:
Andrew Liveris The Dow Chemical Company - Chairman & CEO: Yes, I'll get Jim to handle that one as well, Hassan.
Jim Fitterling The Dow Chemical Company - President & COO: Hassan, what I would say, we have said since the beginning of this -- our long-term experience in the ethylene business is this. Half of what's announced is in play and half of that might come on, on the timeframe that was committed to. So when you look at what's in the first wave today, the things that we know: we know that Braskem Idesa has started up, experiencing a few problems, but has started up. <NEWLINE>You've got three big players: ourselves, CP Chem and Exxon that are coming and a small cracker with OxyChem. That is our view of the first wave of capacity that's coming on. That is quite bit ahead of anybody else. Those were the first ones out of the ground and are going to continue to be the ones you see in the first wave. When the second wave comes is anybody's guess at this point. Some people are saying 2018. I think it might even slide into 2019 or 2020. Given the financial conditions there and given things that are going on with construction labor, I think that would be a realistic expectation. I don't expect a tidal wave of new capacity coming on. We're well-positioned as a first mover in this. In fact, I think we're going to be up before the rest.
